title: Eight limbs
hook: Patanjali's yoga has eight limbs, from how you treat others to absorption (Yoga Sutras 2.29)

segments.voice: Yesterday, prayer as rhythm: salah, five set moments that move with the sun. Your line was a rhythm. When your sunset came, or your noon, did you stop for that one breath? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

On a gym schedule, yoga means a mat and a set of poses. Downward dog, a warrior, a long lie on the floor at the end. Then open an old Sanskrit text called the Yoga Sutras, credited to a teacher named Patanjali, and look for the poses. Posture is there, and the advice is brief: sit steady and at ease. But it's one item on a list, and it isn't the first. The list has eight items. The book calls them limbs. And the first two have nothing to do with stretching at all. Today's word is the list.
screen: `ON A GYM SCHEDULE: A MAT AND POSES.` → `IN THE SUTRAS: ONE ITEM ON A LIST.` → `EIGHT LIMBS.`

segments.voice: Ashtanga: eight limbs. In sutra two twenty-nine, Patanjali names them in order. Yama, restraints. Niyama, observances. Asana, posture. Pranayama, the regulation of breath. Pratyahara, drawing the senses inward. Dharana, concentration. Dhyana, meditation. Samadhi, absorption. Start where the list starts. The very next sutra spells out the restraints: not harming, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint, and not grasping. A little later the book adds that when these are kept everywhere, at every time, in every circumstance, they become a great vow. Then the observances: cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study of oneself, and devotion to the Lord. Before a single pose, the yoga of this book asks how you treat people and what you do with your days. Only then does the body sit down, steady and at ease. Only then does the breath get attention. And then the list turns inward, step by step, until in the last three limbs, which the book calls more inward than the first five, attention narrows to one point, flows there, and is absorbed. Readers take the shape in more than one way. Some teachers read it as a ladder, each limb resting on the one below. Others lean on the word itself: limbs, like the arms and legs of one body, growing together rather than climbed and left behind. The text gives the list; it leaves room for both readings. This week walked through Sufi and Muslim ways: watchfulness, al-Ghazali's crisis, solitude in the crowd, the retreat, the turning of the Mevlevi, and prayer's rhythm. Today the road crosses into Hindu ways, and it starts, of all places, with how to treat people.
screen: `EIGHT LIMBS, NAMED IN ORDER.` · `FIRST, HOW YOU TREAT PEOPLE.` · `THEN BODY AND BREATH.` · `THEN INWARD, TO ABSORPTION.` · then, large: `A LADDER, OR ONE BODY?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the eight limbs. Settle, and let the breath slow. Then go down the list, one limb to a breath, inside or in a whisper. Restraint. Observance. Posture. Breath. Turning inward. Concentration. Meditation. Absorption. When you reach the end, go back to the top and do it again, slower. Notice which limb feels near today, and which feels far away. Don't fix anything. Just notice where the list catches. The bell holds the time.
Ashtanga. Eight limbs, the shape of Patanjali's yoga in the Yoga Sutras: from how you treat others, through body and breath, inward to absorption. Today's word.

Your line: eight limbs. Today, take just the first one, not harming, and keep it for one ordinary hour: in what you say, what you type, and how you speak to yourself. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Students of classical yoga learn Patanjali's eight limbs as a path that begins with ethical restraints and observances, moves through posture and breath, and turns inward toward concentration, meditation and absorption; teachers differ on whether the limbs are steps or parts practiced together.

notes: All Yoga Sutras material paraphrased (no validator-listed public-domain translation). Confirm: 2.29 list and order; 2.30 the five yamas (brahmacharya rendered 'sexual restraint'); 2.31 'great vow' when unlimited by birth, place, time or circumstance (birth left out of the voice for simplicity); 2.32 the niyamas (ishvara pranidhana rendered 'devotion to the Lord'); 2.46 sthira-sukham asanam ('steady and at ease'); 3.7 the three inner limbs.
